# Diaphragmatic injuries

*Categories: Clinical knowledge > Surgery > Abdominal surgery > Hernias > Diaphragmatic injuries*

[Original Article Link](/library/co0aaS)

---

## Summary

Diaphragmatic injury is a penetrating or blunt thoracoabdominal and flank injury in which the continuity of the <u>diaphragm</u> is compromised (e.g., via a tear, perforation, or rupture), resulting in <u>herniation</u> of abdominal contents into the <u>thoracic cavity</u>. While diaphragmatic injuries are often asymptomatic, clinical features range from thoracoabdominal <u>pain</u> and decreased breath sounds to acute <u>respiratory distress</u>. Diagnosis is typically based on CT findings, but <u>diagnostic laparoscopy</u> or <u>thoracoscopy</u> may be required if <u>CT scan</u> is normal and there is a high level of clinical suspicion. Most diaphragmatic injuries require operative repair; nonoperative management may be sufficient for selected patients. Delayed complications of diaphragmatic injuries commonly result from <u>diaphragmatic hernias</u> (e.g., <u>bowel obstruction</u>, <u>strangulated hernia</u>).

---

## Etiology

### Penetrating injury [[6]](/library/-CXDuZ0)[[7]](/library/M1VMht0)




* <u>Epidemiology</u>: 67% of diaphragmatic injuries [[1]](/library/uXWp-P0)

* Mechanism: direct <u>laceration</u> or puncture of the <u>diaphragm</u> by a penetrating object

* Causes

* <u>Gunshot wounds</u>

* <u>Stab injuries</u>

* Rarely, <u>iatrogenic</u> injury (e.g., thoracoabdominal <u>surgery</u>, <u>thoracentesis</u>, ablative procedures) [[2]](/library/K4VU4u0)[[8]](/library/64Vj4u0)

* Characteristics [[7]](/library/M1VMht0)

* Injuries tend to be small (80% are < 2 cm).

* Often missed on initial evaluation





### <u>Blunt abdominal trauma</u> [[6]](/library/-CXDuZ0)[[7]](/library/M1VMht0)




* <u>Epidemiology</u>: 33% of diaphragmatic injuries [[1]](/library/uXWp-P0)

* Mechanism: sudden increase in <u>intra-abdominal pressure</u> causing diaphragmatic rupture

* Causes: <u>motor vehicle collision</u>, falls, <u>crush injuries</u>

* Characteristics

* Defects are usually large radial tears.

* Most common on the left side





> [!TIP]
> Other than <u>hiatal hernias</u>, other spontaneously <u>acquired diaphragmatic hernias</u> (e.g., after weightlifting, <u>valsalva maneuver</u>, or <u>childbirth</u>) without a clear history of trauma are very rare. [[9]](/library/G4VBku0)

---

## Clinical features

While patients are often symptomatic, symptoms vary based on injury size and the presence of complications (e.g., <u>diaphragmatic hernia</u>).




### Acute presentation [[10]](/library/AN1Rdh0)




* Diaphragmatic injury [[11]](/library/I4VYku0) 

* Thoracoabdominal <u>pain</u>

* Thoracoabdominal <u>contusions</u>

* Referred shoulder <u>pain</u>

* Decreased breath sounds

* <u>Diaphragmatic hernia</u> [[11]](/library/I4VYku0)[[12]](/library/r4Vfku0)

* <u>Bowel sounds</u> in the chest

* <u>Respiratory distress</u>

* <u>Symptoms of bowel obstruction</u>

* Symptoms of <u>strangulated hernia</u> (e.g., <u>peritonitis</u>)

* Associated injuries (Isolated diaphragmatic injuries are rare.) [[7]](/library/M1VMht0) 

* Signs of <u>penetrating thoracoabdominal and flank trauma</u>

* Signs of <u>blunt abdominal trauma</u>





### Delayed presentation




Delayed symptoms most often result from <u>herniation</u> of abdominal contents through an initially unrecognized diaphragmatic defect, rather than from the injury itself.




* Nonspecific abdominal <u>pain</u>

* Retrosternal <u>pain</u> and pressure

* Cardiopulmonary symptoms (e.g., <u>dyspnea</u>, <u>tachycardia</u>, <u>arrhythmias</u>)

* Complications of diaphragmatic injury

---

## Diagnosis

### Approach [[1]](/library/uXWp-P0)[[7]](/library/M1VMht0)[[13]](/library/n1V7ht0)




* Acute presentation

* Obtain portable <u>chest x-ray</u> and <u>FAST</u> as adjuncts to the <u>primary survey</u>. [[14]](/library/ohV0U80)

* Blunt thoracoabdominal trauma: <u>CT scan for diaphragmatic injury</u>

* <u>Penetrating thoracoabdominal and flank trauma</u> 

* Right-sided: <u>CT scan for diaphragmatic injury</u>

* Left-sided: <u>CT scan for diaphragmatic injury</u> or <u>diagnostic laparoscopy</u>

* Delayed presentation: <u>CT scan for diaphragmatic injury</u>





> [!WARNING]
> Begin urgent management if indications for <u>emergency exploratory laparotomy</u> are identified during the <u>primary survey</u>.




### <u>Chest x-ray</u>




* Poor <u>sensitivity</u> for evaluating diaphragmatic injuries

* Findings [[15]](/library/ZydZds0)

* Abnormal <u>diaphragm</u> contour

* Elevated hemidiaphragm

* Bowel in thorax (e.g., <u>air-fluid levels</u>)

* <u>Nasogastric tube</u> in thorax





> [!WARNING]
> <u>Chest x-ray</u> findings of diaphragmatic injury may be misinterpreted as an elevated hemidiaphragm, <u>loculated</u> <u>pneumothorax</u>, or subpulmonic <u>hematoma</u>. [[7]](/library/M1VMht0)




![Posttraumatic diaphragmatic hernia simulating diaphragm elevation](media/gy9ycli7jjy598qkd2vunu1x.jpg)

Posttraumatic diaphragmatic hernia simulating diaphragm elevation




### CT scan for diaphragmatic injury [[15]](/library/ZydZds0)




The choice of CT imaging varies based on suspected concomitant injuries (see "<u>CT scan in trauma</u>") and suspected complications of diaphragmatic injuries (e.g., <u>strangulated hernia</u>).




* Protocols

* CT chest with IV contrast

* CT abdomen and <u>pelvis</u> with IV contrast

* CT chest, abdomen, and <u>pelvis</u> with IV contrast

* Findings

* Discontinuity of <u>diaphragm</u>

* Abdominal <u>viscera</u> in thorax

* <u>Nasogastric tube</u> in thorax

* Collar sign: band-like constriction of herniated abdominal organs at the level of the diaphragmatic defect





> [!WARNING]
> <u>Positive pressure ventilation</u> can temporarily reduce herniated contents, causing diaphragmatic injuries to be missed on imaging. Maintain a high level of suspicion in ventilated patients with thoracoabdominal trauma, even if <u>CT scan</u> is negative. [[16]](/library/o1V03t0)




![Traumatic diaphragmatic hernia](media/sv8bmertm230ragt7pq0rpfb.jpg)

Traumatic diaphragmatic hernia




### <u>Laparoscopy</u> or <u>thoracoscopy</u>




<u>Laparoscopy</u> or <u>thoracoscopy</u> is used for diagnostic confirmation and therapeutic intervention.




* Indications

* High clinical suspicion despite negative CT imaging

* Suspected associated injuries requiring surgical exploration

* Alternative to <u>CT scan</u> for left <u>thoracoabdominal penetrating trauma</u>

* Findings

* Discontinuity of <u>diaphragm</u>

* Abdominal organs in thorax

---

## Differential diagnoses

* <u>Pneumothorax</u>

* <u>Hiatal hernia</u>

* <u>Congenital diaphragmatic hernia</u>

* <u>Phrenic nerve</u> palsy




The differential diagnoses listed here are not exhaustive.

---

## Management

Management of diaphragmatic injuries is guided by hemodynamic stability, the side of the injury (left vs. right), and the mechanism of injury. [[1]](/library/uXWp-P0)




### Approach [[1]](/library/uXWp-P0)




* Acute presentation

* Initial management 

* Follow <u>ATLS</u> protocols (see "<u>Management of trauma patients</u>").

* Identify indications for <u>emergency exploratory laparotomy</u>.

* Obtain early trauma or surgical consultation for all suspected diaphragmatic injuries.

* <u>Blunt trauma</u>: operative repair

* Left-sided <u>penetrating trauma</u>: operative repair

* Right-sided <u>penetrating trauma</u>: nonoperative or operative repair  [[1]](/library/uXWp-P0)

* Delayed presentation

* Uncomplicated <u>hernias</u>: elective operative repair

* Complicated <u>hernias</u> (e.g., <u>strangulated hernia</u>): urgent operative repair with <u>bowel resection</u> if needed





> [!WARNING]
> Exercise caution when inserting a <u>chest tube</u> in patients with suspected <u>diaphragm</u> injuries to prevent injuring herniated abdominal contents. [[7]](/library/M1VMht0)




### Operative management [[1]](/library/uXWp-P0)




* Surgical approaches

* Abdominal: (e.g., <u>laparoscopy</u>, <u>laparotomy</u>)

* Thoracic: (e.g., <u>thoracoscopy</u>, <u>thoracotomy</u>)

* The choice of surgical approach depends on associated injuries.

* Abdominal approach is preferred over thoracic approach. [[1]](/library/uXWp-P0)

* <u>Laparoscopic</u> repair is preferred over open repair for isolated penetrating diaphragmatic injuries. [[1]](/library/uXWp-P0)





![Intraoperative view of a diaphragmatic perforation](media/pntd6vxrc3n4kot933d12yns.jpg)

Intraoperative view of a diaphragmatic perforation




### Nonoperative management [[1]](/library/uXWp-P0)




* May be considered if all of the following criteria are met:

* Right-sided <u>thoracoabdominal penetrating trauma</u>

* Patient is hemodynamically stable

* No <u>diaphragmatic hernia</u>

* No <u>peritonitis</u>

* Management typically includes:

* Monitoring (e.g., <u>vital signs</u>, <u>serial abdominal examinations</u>)

* <u>Supportive care</u> (e.g., <u>antiemetics</u>, <u>analgesia</u>)

* Outpatient surgical follow-up

---

## Complications

### Acute complications [[7]](/library/M1VMht0)




* Respiratory compromise

* <u>Hemothorax</u>

* <u>Cardiac tamponade</u>  [[17]](/library/L1Vwht0)

* <u>Diaphragm paralysis</u>





### Delayed complications




* <u>Herniation</u> with <u>visceral</u> complications, e.g.:

* <u>Bowel obstruction</u>

* <u>Bowel perforation</u>

* <u>Strangulated hernia</u>

* <u>Gastric volvulus</u>

* Progressive enlargement of the defect





We list the most important complications. The selection is not exhaustive.
